title: Call for more mental health supports renewed in wake of police shooting
article: The police shooting death of a man with a machete in Windsor's core has downtown councillor Rino Bortolin again asking why funding for mental health is so hard to come by.

Shifting blame away from the officer who fatally shot 70-year-old Allan Andkilde on Monday afternoon, Bortolin told the Star the situation could have been prevented if adequate mental health supports had been available prior to the "enormously tragic" event.

"We're years behind on this and people are literally dying on our streets," Bortolin said. "We're not taking action. We know what the action is. We need mental health money. We need addictions beds. It's that simple."

As a member of the Windsor Police Services Board, Bortolin said growing gaps in the mental health system over the last few decades have been filled by law enforcement. A "huge chunk" of calls for police service are not crime-related but are about social issues, with costly police resources spent driving people without homes to emergency shelters, and people in crisis to hospitals for support.

"Situations like the one on Monday highlight what dire consequences we can have if we're relying on police to do these things," he said. "That's not to say police did anything wrong. The issue is, why was that person in that position, in that state, in that location?"

Windsor police have a partnership with Hôtel-Dieu Grace Healthcare called the Windsor Mobile Crisis Rapid Response Team, which sees two crisis intervention-trained officers and two dedicated crisis intervention-trained mental health social workers making up two units. According to the hospital's website, the team's job is to respond to dispatched calls to "individuals who present with symptoms of mental illness, substance abuse, behavioural disorders, or people in acute crisis situations."
But that team's resources are limited and it wouldn't have been much help to Andkilde on Monday, Bortolin said.
"What you saw on Monday was a person well past the point of normal de-escalation. This was a person that was violent, had a history of (violence) - that's not where (the crisis team) fits in."

Bortolin said he and "a lot of people" living and working downtown were familiar with Andkilde, who reportedly wielded a machete and threatened people at the intersection of Wyandotte Street and Ouellette Avenue at about 2:30 p.m. According to Ontario's Special Investigations Unit, which has taken over the investigation, once Windsor police located Andkilde, there was an "interaction" between him and the officers during which one deployed a conducted energy weapon and another officer shot him.
Paramedics transported Andkilde to hospital where he was pronounced deceased.

"A competent and very successful constable had to take those measures and now needs to live with that action for the rest of his life," Bortolin said, noting how police are being put in "impossible" situations. "We as a society... It's almost as if we're okay with this happening.

"We need large amounts of provincial funding to make up for the gaps in mental health supports today. We needed it yesterday, we needed it a year ago, we needed it two years ago, but we need it today."
SIU continues to investigate the shooting and asks that anyone with information, including video or photos, contact the lead investigator at 1-800-787-8529 or siu.on.ca/en/appeals.php.
